source: Rowe & Wright (1999) The Delphi technique as a forecasting tool: issues and analysis
finding: Vote-count review of lab studies: Delphi groups beat statistical (averaged) groups and standard interacting groups, but there is no consistent edge over other structured group methods.
numbers: Delphi beat statistical groups in 12 studies vs 2 (2 ties); beat standard interacting groups in 5 vs 1 (2 ties). Read from abstract snippet only.
limits: Lab Delphi differs from the original concept (expertise, feedback type uncontrolled). Abstract only, full text not read.
agent_relevance: Structured rounds help over one-shot averaging, but a plain nominal-group protocol is a fair rival. Test rounds against simple averaging.

source: Wikipedia: Delphi method (Basu & Schroeder 1977 case; Sackman 1974 critique)
finding: Page reports one business case where Delphi predicted two-year new-product sales within 3-4% error, against 10-15% for quantitative methods and about 20% for unstructured forecasts. It also says overall accuracy is mixed, and gives no pooled accuracy or replication rate.
numbers: Basu & Schroeder (1977) single case: 3-4% vs 10-15% vs about 20%. No meta-analysis figures on the page.
limits: One case, secondary source. Sackman (RAND R-1283-PR, 1974) is cited as critic with no numbers on the page.
agent_relevance: Delphi evidence is thin and case-based. Do not treat Delphi as proven; use it as a protocol to test.

source: Wikipedia: Delphi method (speed and online variants)
finding: Fast-track Delphi gives results in about three weeks against months or years; large online Delphis exist.
numbers: eLAC: five-round Delphi with 1,454 contributions; TechCast panel about 100 experts; fast-track about 3 weeks.
limits: Secondary summary. Reports no accuracy gain from the speed-up.
agent_relevance: Cheap and fast rounds are the one clear advantage an LLM panel copies; it says nothing yet about accuracy.

source: Wikipedia: Herman Kahn (RAND scenarios, The Year 2000)
finding: Kahn's RAND scenario work used stories of escalation; the Year 2000 book (1967, with Wiener) listed 100 'very likely' technical innovations. The page gives no accuracy audit.
numbers: Escalation ladder: 16 steps (1962) grown to 44 (1965). Year 2000 Table XVIII: 100 innovations. Predicted Japan passes US per-capita income by 1990 (page does not say if true).
limits: No scoring of Kahn's forecasts is given. Reception was mixed; critics called On Thermonuclear War a moral tract on mass murder.
agent_relevance: Narrative scenarios were never scored against outcomes. If our agent writes scenarios, score them with a rubric, not by fluency.

source: Wikipedia: Morphological analysis (problem solving)
finding: Zwicky's method splits a problem into parameters with options, then removes illogical pairs by cross-consistency assessment (CCA). Page gives no empirical test of whether it improves solutions.
numbers: Worked example: 6 parameters x 4 options each. Ritchey (1998) general morphological analysis cited.
limits: No evaluation data, combinatorial explosion numbers or criticisms on the page.
agent_relevance: The box plus consistency check is a code-checkable step (enumerate, prune), which fits our program-decides rule. No outcome evidence.

source: Bertolotti & Mari (2025) An LLM-based Delphi study to predict GenAI evolution
finding: gpt-4o-mini played Delphi panelists and an organiser agent for 5 rounds on the future of generative AI. Themes appeared across runs but depended on starting questions and panel size.
numbers: 12 experiments: 5 or 15 responding agents x 5 or 15 responses each; 3 repeats; temperature 0.7; Likert 1-5; question lists pruned by embedding similarity.
limits: No ground truth, no accuracy score. Fixed 5 rounds, no consensus stop. Authors report knowledge cutoff, bias and sensitivity to initial conditions.
agent_relevance: LLM Delphi gives breadth of topics, not shown accuracy. Run-to-run spread is large, so repeat runs and keep only themes that recur.

source: Bertolotti & Mari (2025), topic coverage table
finding: Across the 12 runs a few themes (geopolitics, economics, regulation, education) show up in all or almost all runs, while others (data, sustainability, psychology) appear in only some.
numbers: Table 1: 14 topics x 12 runs; yes/no occurrence, e.g. run 1 has 9 of 14 topics, run 9 has 10 of 14 (my tally of the printed table). Early topics always appeared first.
limits: Small sample of 12 runs; counts are my reading of the table.
agent_relevance: Use recurrence across independent runs as a cheap stability filter for scenario themes.

source: Barrett et al. (2025) Assessing confidence in frontier AI safety cases
finding: Fully LLM Delphi: 50 gpt-4o-mini experts over 40 roles, max 5 rounds, stop when spread under 10 points. On selected forecasting questions it was better calibrated than Metaculus, with less extreme probabilities.
numbers: N=50 experts, temperature 1.5 (works for 1 to 1.75), consensus threshold SD<10%; spread vs correctness across 100 scenarios p=0.053 (Mann-Whitney).
limits: Small hand-picked question set; Metaculus snapshot up to 6 months after the LLM's information; no confidence interval on the calibration claim in the text; p=0.053 is not significant at 0.05.
agent_relevance: High panel spread flagged wrong answers (weakly). A program can use panel spread as an uncertainty signal and escalate.

source: Lorenz & Fritz (2026) Scalable Delphi: LLMs for structured risk estimation
finding: LLM persona panels (5 experts, with feedback rounds) predicted agent success rates on three security benchmarks with Pearson r 0.91-0.98 once given full evidence.
numbers: MAE 4.5-6.1 pp, ECE 1.6-4.1 pp. GPT-5.1: r 0.97/0.97/0.91, Opus-4.1: 0.95/0.98/0.93. Llama-4 Maverick (no extended reasoning) r=0.74 on Cybench, MAE 10.8. Baseline mean-of-others error 12.3/20.0/16.7 pp. Plausibility ranges contain truth only 39-80%.
limits: Proxy ground truth only; benchmark data may be in training data; ranges are not calibrated intervals.
agent_relevance: Accuracy rides on the evidence package. Our agent should hand panelists briefing facts and ablate them to check sensitivity.

source: Lorenz & Fritz (2026), evidence ablation
finding: With agent and benchmark identity hidden, panel estimates were near noise or negative; adding both lifted correlation to about 0.92-0.97. Benchmark description alone barely helped.
numbers: Anonymised r: BountyBench 0.30, Cybench -0.22, CyberGym -0.40; full information r 0.97 (Cybench), 0.92 (CyberGym).
limits: Within-task correlation, three benchmarks.
agent_relevance: The panel is an evidence aggregator, not an oracle. Pass the evidence, not just the question.

source: Lorenz & Fritz (2026), expert alignment (Murray et al. 2025 cyber panel)
finding: GPT-5.1 panel matched human panel A better than the two human panels matched each other. Opus-4.1 ran higher.
numbers: Mean abs diff: human A vs B 16.6 pp; GPT-5.1 vs A 5.0 pp; Opus-4.1 vs A 12.8 pp. Easy task 27-34%, hard task 38-82%.
limits: Human panels disagree a lot, so matching humans is a loose target. Small panels (n=5 LLM, n=14 human).
agent_relevance: Which base model you use shifts the answer by more than which persona; vary models, not just personas.

source: Lorenz & Fritz (2026), long-horizon divergence (Bamber et al. 2019 ice sheets)
finding: On a 2019 expert study of ice-sheet sea-level rise (22 experts), LLM panels matched near-term medians but fell to about half the human median at long horizons.
numbers: 2050 high-warming: LLM medians about 65 mm vs human 120 mm. At 2300 the two LLMs differed by 2.6x. Re-running with post-2018 data moved GPT-5.1 medians down 11-28%.
limits: Study predates model cutoffs, so contamination cannot be excluded. Human panel resampled from n=14 to n=5.
agent_relevance: LLM panels fail first on far extrapolation and counts. Flag long-horizon items for extra checks.

source: Lorenz & Fritz (2026), variance and persona effects
finding: Panel spread is squeezed and only partly tracks real uncertainty. Base model matters more than persona. Humans and LLMs both converge toward the panel mean across rounds.
numbers: Persona effect 2.4 pp vs model effect 4.8 pp (after mediation 0.5 vs 4.4). Numeric convergence: Opus 0.49 to 0.19, humans 0.73 to 0.55, GPT 0.10 to 0.08. Rationale length: humans 234 chars, Opus 414, GPT 736.
limits: Three studies, single run each; an LLM judge labels reasoning patterns.
agent_relevance: Use first-round spread and cross-model disagreement as uncertainty signals, not final panel spread.

source: Barrett et al. (2025) Toward quantitative modeling of cybersecurity risks due to AI misuse (SaferAI)
finding: Human modified Delphi (9 experts) vs LLM simulated Delphi on one risk model: probability factors close, quantity factors far apart. The authors state extra LLM rounds did not improve predictions.
numbers: LLM probability estimates within 6% of humans on average, never over 15%; quantities lower by up to 70%. Human coherence to consensus ranged 0.08-0.8, mean 0.38. LLM spread lower than humans.
limits: Only one of nine risk models had a human comparison. No ground truth. The round claim is a remark in the limitations, not a measured experiment.
agent_relevance: Do not buy extra Delphi rounds for LLM panels; spend on diverse models and evidence. Expect LLM panels to under-estimate quantities.

source: Barrett et al. (2025), monotonicity of LLM estimates
finding: Human uplift estimates rise with task difficulty; LLM estimates were jagged and sometimes lower for harder tasks, which breaks a logic constraint stated in the prompt.
numbers: Qualitative figure (total risk by task difficulty); no summary statistic given.
limits: Could reflect a better task-difficulty sense than the authors' ordering.
agent_relevance: Add a code check for monotone and ordered estimates across related items.

source: Peristiani, Morgan & Savino (2010/2014) Information value of the stress test and bank opacity (NY Fed SR 460)
finding: Event study of the 2009 US bank stress test (SCAP, 19 banks). The market had mostly guessed which banks had gaps, but bank returns still moved with the size of the gap, so the test added information.
numbers: 19 banks; 9 GAP and 9 NO-GAP banks compared. Aggregate gap $75bn vs consensus $100-200bn. Adverse scenario: GDP -3.3% in 2009, house prices -22%, unemployment 8.9%. Significant abnormal returns for GAP banks, not for NO-GAP.
limits: One episode, event-study identification; tied to a simultaneous government backstop (clarification that banks would not be nationalised).
agent_relevance: A stress test works when paired with credible disclosure and a response. For our agent: severity assumptions must be stated openly.

source: Soleimani (2026) LLM-generated counterfactual stress scenarios for portfolio risk (v2)
finding: 2,420 accepted G7 scenarios from GPT-5.6-luna and Llama-3.1-8B. Severity came from the prompt, not the model: prompt variant explains most variance.
numbers: Prompt variant partial eta-sq 0.87 (GPT, Portfolio A) and about 0.40 (Llama); country 0.09-0.14. Removing severity bands made recession 1.6 pp milder (-3.85 to -2.20 pp) and linear VaR multiples fell 17%, CVaR 15%.
limits: Authors say eta-sq 0.87 is inflated by design and the cross-model comparison is confounded. Macro-to-factor map is stipulated, not estimated.
agent_relevance: LLM scenarios copy the severity you tell them. Fix severity by rule and let the model write narrative and sectors.

source: Soleimani (2026), model consistency and reproducibility
finding: The small open model was much more dispersed and contradicted its own stated changes. A repeat run differed per scenario but agreed on the aggregate.
numbers: Llama within-tier spread 4-7x GPT's; contradicts own stated changes in 90% of cases. Repeat run agreed on aggregate multiples to within 0.007x.
limits: Llama-3.1-8B only; NLI classifier for narrative severity not validated against experts.
agent_relevance: Check numbers against the text with code; trust aggregates over single scenarios.

source: Soleimani (2026), narrative vs numeric severity and retrieval
finding: A scenario can read as a catastrophe yet carry a mild number. Retrieval and news changed nothing in tail risk when prompts fixed magnitude.
numbers: Association between growth shock and narrative severity about zero in severe and systemic tiers (three quarters of the corpus); unanchored run r=+0.014; contained tier GPT corr -0.85 after range-restriction correction. Retrieval null in every run. Plausibility gate rejects 0.2%.
limits: Weak coupling may be attenuated by measurement error. Null for retrieval attributed to a narrow corpus.
agent_relevance: Never let story severity stand in for a computed number. Keep a code check linking the two.

source: Fruhling et al. (2026) Agent-supported foresight for AI systemic risks (Futures Wheel, CHI '26)
finding: LLM agents ran Futures Wheels (consequence trees) for four AI uses. Thematic coverage was stable across runs, and agents generated more systemic consequences than humans.
numbers: 30 agent runs; 86-110 consequences per run reduced to 27-47 unique risks; 6 agents per wheel; theme similarity above 0.95 across runs; 290 domain experts and 7 leaders rated; human sessions with 42 experts and 42 laypeople. LLM-vs-human labelling agreement weighted F1 0.86 (0.96 for risk class).
limits: Agents skewed over 90% negative (risks not benefits). GPT-4.1 mini only. Humans' own systemic share can be as low as 24%.
agent_relevance: LLM agents widen the scenario list; humans judge likelihood. Split the roles: model for breadth, code and checks for pruning.

source: Fruhling et al. (2026), agents vs humans on systemic share and likelihood
finding: Agent-listed risks were mostly judged systemic (domain experts 93%, leaders about 75%); humans listed fewer risks, less systemic but judged more likely. Leaders flagged generic items.
numbers: Systemic share of risks per use case in the table: agents 84-100% vs human-only domain experts 24-63%. Leaders marked 58% to 92% as consequential depending on use case. Humans found agent risks harder to understand at low technology readiness.
limits: Share numbers read from a figure table; classification by LLM judge plus humans.
agent_relevance: Expect LLM scenario lists to be broad but generic. Add a specificity filter.

source: Barnett, Kieslich & Diakopoulos (2024) Generative scenario writing to evaluate regulation (AIES)
finding: GPT-4 wrote paired scenarios (without and with a transparency law). 234 raters judged the law as mildly lowering severity, with plausibility unchanged.
numbers: n=234 raters; mean severity 3.66 (SD 1.08), plausibility 3.94; severity change -0.38 (SD 1.01, p<0.001); 40% of scenarios lower in severity; plausibility change -0.03 (p<0.05). GPT-4 failed to depict 39 impact types when prompted.
limits: Perceived effects only, not real policy outcomes; one law, one taxonomy; GPT-4 prompts failed for some impact types.
agent_relevance: A before/after scenario pair with checked ratings is a testable form of scenario use.

source: Preserving Disagreement (2026) AI Council: heterogeneity in multi-agent policy simulation
finding: Giving each value perspective a different model cut first-choice concentration (artificial consensus) compared with one model for all.
numbers: 120 deliberations, two scenarios. Child welfare 70.9% to 46.1% (p<0.001, r=0.58); housing 46.0% to 22.9% (p<0.001, r=0.50). Coherence validation: 46.1% to 40.8% (p=0.004) in one, 22.9% to 26.6% (p=0.96) in the other. About half of value conflicts trustworthy.
limits: Small 7-9B models; two scenarios; heterogeneity effect can reverse on accuracy tasks (cited work).
agent_relevance: Delphi-style convergence is a defect for scenario work. Use mixed models and protect minority views.

source: Evidence-grounded social-weighted persona panel for generative UI evaluation (2026)
finding: A persona panel with Delphi-style weighting tracked human ratings far better than one LLM judge. Most of the gain came from the panel and evidence grounding, not from the discussion step.
numbers: Pearson r: single judge 0.716, prompt-ensemble 0.789, full 0.922. Ablation: no dynamics 0.891, no grounding 0.811. Discussion cut spread 0.283 to 0.134 but only 42.6% of panels fully converged.
limits: Different task (UI ratings), not forecasting; Delphi only inspires the weighting.
agent_relevance: Panel diversity plus grounding beat repeated sampling; the discussion round adds little (agrees with b14).

source: Ritchey (1998) General morphological analysis
finding: Standard reference for computer-supported morphological analysis (cross-consistency assessment). Not opened; cited on the Wikipedia page.
numbers: None read.
limits: I know of no outcome evidence that it improves decisions; not verified.
agent_relevance: Treat morphological analysis as an enumerate-and-prune tool; no empirical backing for our agent.

source: Dalkey & Helmer (1963) An experimental application of the Delphi method to the use of experts
finding: Founding RAND Delphi study, cited by the sources above as the origin of rounds with anonymous feedback. Not opened.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not verified here beyond citation.
agent_relevance: Cite as origin only.
